The evaluation covers eight principal benchmarks and includes matched-size random and ICONS baselines as well as full LLaVA-665K training. Achieving broadly comparable aggregate performance with 65K rather than 665K samples is practically promising.

The data-scale, balanced-versus-unbalanced complexity, complexity-range, capability-removal, and instruction-tuning-ratio studies are useful attempts to investigate the proposed design rather than reporting only a single headline result.

The manuscript is generally well organized, includes generation and verification prompts, provides qualitative data examples, and candidly notes limitations associated with closed-model generation and knowledge-intensive tasks.
weaknesses: The central quantity—the number of required capabilities k—is neither well defined nor independently validated. Capabilities such as object recognition, counting, color, spatial recognition, and scene understanding overlap and are rarely atomic. The same Gemini-2.0-Flash model generates examples, supplies its own confidence, verifies that they require exactly k capabilities, and labels evaluation questions. No human audit, inter-annotator agreement, or validation against an independent model is provided, creating substantial correlated-error and circularity risks.

There is a serious taxonomy inconsistency: the appendix capability-analysis prompt replaces the paper's 'scene understanding' capability with an otherwise undefined 'object relationship' capability, although the reported distributions and examples use scene understanding. Moreover, displayed samples contradict the exact-k premise: for example, 'How many green motorcycles are visible?' omits the plainly required object-recognition capability, while a question explicitly saying 'on the city street' is labeled as requiring scene understanding. These issues undermine the complexity distributions, ablations, and complexity-stratified conclusions.

The evidence does not establish compositional generalization in the usual systematic sense. There is no held-out capability-combination split or evaluation on a dedicated controlled compositional benchmark. Instead, two ordinary benchmarks are partitioned post hoc using the same unvalidated Gemini labels. The plotted k>=4 strata have very little probability mass, yet exact sample counts, confidence intervals, and significance tests are omitted; consequently, the headline 83.3% and 94.0% improvements may be dominated by very small subsets.

The primary aggregate result is weak evidence for outperforming full visual instruction tuning: COMPACT's normalized score is 100.18% versus 100.00%, it improves on only four of eight benchmarks, and it substantially degrades MME, TextVQA, CV-Bench, and LLaVA-W. Results are reported from no stated repeated training runs or random seeds, and the shaded regions in several plots are unexplained.

The experiments use only one relatively old model/backbone configuration, LLaVA-v1.5-7B with LoRA. There is no evidence that the recipe transfers across model families, parameter scales, or modern MLLMs, and comparisons to composition-oriented or stronger synthetic-instruction methods are missing.

The causal attribution to compositional balance remains incomplete. Generated datasets can differ in teacher quality, question difficulty, information density, answer distribution, and number of tokens or QA turns. The unbalanced and range ablations do not report controls for these factors, while the leave-one-capability-out experiment necessarily changes correlated capability distributions. A clean unconstrained-Gemini synthetic-data control is needed.

Reproducibility and efficiency claims are incomplete: the exact Gemini snapshot, decoding settings, API cost, rejection rate, random seeds, detailed training/evaluation settings, and generated dataset are not supplied. Counting only final training samples also ignores repeated closed-model generation and verification calls, so the claimed end-to-end compute or cost efficiency is unsubstantiated.

Several unresolved presentation errors reduce confidence, including an appendix reference to 'Figs. 12, 13, and ??', inconsistent MMStar score formatting, and the statement that 32K is eight times 2K. Overall, the idea is promising, but the validity of the core complexity measurement and the evidence for compositional generalization require major revision.

strengths: The paper addresses an important problem: improving the compositional capability and data efficiency of multimodal instruction tuning. The proposed atomic-to-complex data-generation recipe is intuitive and practically relevant.

weaknesses: The central complexity measure is insufficiently validated. Gemini assigns capabilities from question text alone, with no human annotation study, agreement analysis, or audit of label accuracy. Moreover, the disclosed analysis prompt uses a different taxonomy: it introduces “object relationship” and omits the paper's “scene understanding” capability. This directly undermines the reported complexity distributions and high-k evaluation.

The experiments do not establish systematic compositional generalization. There is no controlled split over held-out capability combinations, and greater annotated k on unrelated benchmark questions does not demonstrate generalization to unseen compositions. Exact sample counts and uncertainty are also absent for the rare k=4 and k=5 strata, making dramatic relative improvements—especially 20 versus 0 at k=5—potentially unstable.

The comparison confounds compositional complexity with Gemini-generated data quality, benchmark-aligned wording, capability-frequency balancing, and conversation structure. A quality- and token-matched synthetic baseline without controlled composition is missing. The unbalanced-COMPACT ablation helps but does not isolate these factors.

Generation, verification, and downstream complexity annotation all rely on Gemini-2.0-Flash, so correlated teacher errors are likely despite the verification step being described as independent. Several displayed samples themselves have questionable labels—for example, a static screen reflection is classified as object interaction despite the prompt requiring an active object—and there is no human quality evaluation.

The data-efficiency accounting is ambiguous because “samples,” images, conversation pairs, tokens, and optimization compute are not distinguished. The method collects multiple conversations per image, while the paper reports efficiency primarily through dataset-record counts; the stated 16K dataset is also associated with 96K capability-stratified conversations without a clear accounting.

The empirical scope is limited to one older 7B LoRA backbone and apparently one training run. Main results have no standard deviations, confidence intervals, or significance tests, although many differences are small and COMPACT remains below the full baseline on four of eight benchmarks. Averaging normalized scores into 100.18% does not by itself establish robust superiority.

There are consequential reporting inconsistencies: the text gives conflicting results for the complexity-range ablation, calls 32K versus 2K “eight times” more data, and Figure 3's caption suggests consistent superiority to full VIT even though several plotted results remain below it. The abstract's 94% MM-Vet high-complexity gain is not transparently derivable from the disclosed per-k results, and the appendix contains an unresolved figure reference.

Reproducibility remains limited by the closed teacher, incomplete API and decoding details, underspecified training/evaluation settings, absence of released code or data at submission time, and no analysis of possible benchmark-image overlap or contamination. These issues, together with the unvalidated evaluation construct, prevent the otherwise promising idea from meeting the evidentiary standard of a top-tier venue.

No repeated training runs, confidence intervals, or significance tests support the small 100.18% aggregate result.

The displayed dataset examples directly undermine the proposed verification mechanism. As rendered in Figure 12, “What is the overall setting of this image?” and an action-recognition question both have the answer “Two”; the latter is also labeled as requiring counting despite not asking for a count. Several Figure 13 capability annotations are similarly questionable. No post-filter human accuracy estimate is reported.

Generality is limited to one dated 7B LLaVA architecture, one source dataset, and one training regime. The open-source-generator variant reaches only 98.31% of the paper's aggregate full-data score, while knowledge-intensive tasks and several individual benchmarks show appreciable regressions.

The amount and mixture of training data appear to be selected according to performance on the same benchmark suite used for final reporting, without a held-out model-selection protocol, creating a risk of test-suite overfitting.

Reproducibility and comparison fairness remain insufficient: the generated dataset and code are promised rather than supplied, the primary teacher is proprietary, and implementation details for the numerous pruning baselines, training seeds, evaluator variability, and exact hyperparameters are incomplete. Overall, the empirical signal is promising but does not adequately support the paper's broad efficiency and causal claims at a top-tier acceptance threshold.

The reported data efficiency is potentially valuable: 65K mixed examples attain a reported mean relative score of 100.18% against training on all 665K LLaVA examples, with notable gains on InfoVQA, MM-Vet, MMStar, and SeedBench2Plus.

The evaluation covers eight benchmarks and includes several useful analyses: data scaling, complexity-distribution matching, capability removal, complexity-range variation, instruction-data ratio, token counts, and knowledge-intensive tasks.
Testing Qwen3-VL-4B as an open-source generator is a welcome robustness check; although weaker than Gemini, it still improves substantially over the equally sized random-data baseline.
The appendix discloses prompts, generation cost, filtering criteria, and recognized failure modes, which is more transparent than many synthetic-data papers.
weaknesses: The central causal interpretation is insufficiently established. Gemini-2.0-Flash generates the questions and answers, assigns confidence, verifies capability use, and annotates k for much of the analysis. Without an independent human audit or separate verifier, the complexity measurements and quality checks are circular and may primarily reflect the teacher model's own biases.

The claimed 100.18% performance is an unweighted average of relative scores across heterogeneous metrics and hides substantial regressions on four of eight benchmarks: approximately 6.7% on MME, 5.6% on TextVQA, 9.3% on CV-Bench, and 5.8% on LLaVA-in-the-Wild relative to full-data training. Thus, statements that COMPACT matches full training broadly or “across benchmarks” are overstated.

The k-value is not convincingly validated as a general complexity measure. Its ten capabilities are overlapping and arbitrarily granular, object recognition is often implicitly assumed, and the main validation uses Gemini-derived labels. The TextVQA evidence is observational, has only 2.2% k=3 examples, excludes k>=4, and provides no uncertainty or control for other difficulty factors.

The comparisons do not isolate complexity from synthetic-supervision quality, answer concision, or question style. COMPACT receives new Gemini-generated labels while pruning baselines retain original LLaVA data. The matched-distribution experiment itself shows that roughly half of the improvement over random selection remains attributable to factors other than increased k, yet these factors are not disentangled.

The study uses only one student architecture and scale, LLaVA-v1.5-7B with LoRA. No training seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests are reported, and the bands in the scaling plot are unexplained. This is inadequate for small aggregate differences such as 100.18% versus 100%.

The paper's own qualitative examples reveal serious quality-control or figure-assembly problems: Figure 12 answers “Two” to “What is the overall setting of this image?” and to an action-recognition question, while one example marked k=5 lists six capabilities. These errors directly undermine confidence in the generated dataset and its automatic verification.

Reproducibility remains incomplete. The data and code are only promised for future release, the provided generation and verification prompts omit important output-format and confidence-scoring details described in the method, and the training/evaluation configurations are largely delegated to unspecified “official” settings.

Overall, the recipe is promising and empirically interesting, but the limited generality, circular validation, lack of statistical reliability, misleading aggregate claim, and visible label-quality failures prevent the work from meeting the technical-evidence bar of a top-tier venue.

strengths: The paper addresses an important practical problem and proposes a simple, intuitive recipe for increasing the compositional content of visual-instruction data.
Evaluation covers eight benchmarks and several data-pruning baselines. COMPACT improves over the equal-size random subset on every reported metric and usually outperforms the pruning methods.
The capability-range, instruction-mixture, and generator analyses are useful. Providing prompts, approximate generation cost, token statistics, and acknowledged failure modes improves transparency.
The main paper is generally understandable, and the method could be practically useful if validated more rigorously.
weaknesses: The headline claim of retaining 100.2% of full-data performance relies on an unweighted mean of per-benchmark ratios that masks substantial regressions. Relative to full LLaVA-665K training, COMPACT is worse on four of eight benchmarks, including MME (1379.94 vs. 1478.48), TextVQA (44.37 vs. 46.99), CV-Bench (55.28 vs. 60.92), and LLaVA-W (64.50 vs. 68.50). No repeated runs, confidence intervals, or significance tests establish that the small aggregate difference is meaningful.

The comparison confounds compositional complexity with teacher-generated data quality, concise answer formatting, capability balancing, and possible distillation from Gemini. Most baselines merely select existing LLaVA data and therefore receive no comparable synthetic regeneration. In Table 3, higher-complexity COMPACT improves over the complexity-matched synthetic control on only three of eight individual benchmarks, despite the claimed aggregate attribution to higher k.

The proposed k-value is not convincingly validated as a measure of complexity or information density. The taxonomy is overlapping and hierarchical, each capability is weighted equally, and the same Gemini model generates, verifies, and later labels the data. There is no independent human annotation, agreement study, or residual-error audit. The TextVQA correlation analysis is observational and confounded by different question distributions.

The evaluation uses only one relatively old LLaVA-v1.5-7B LoRA student and one checkpoint. There is no evidence that the recipe transfers across model families, scales, full finetuning, or modern stronger MLLMs. The open-source-generator variant also falls below full-data performance overall.

Important recipe choices appear selected using the reported evaluation benchmarks: the compositional-data size is explicitly chosen as the minimum needed to match full-data performance, while the instruction-mixture ratio is tuned on overlapping benchmarks. Without a separate validation suite or held-out capability combinations, the headline result is vulnerable to benchmark-level overfitting and does not demonstrate compositional generalization.

The qualitative appendix itself reveals serious quality-control failures. For example, “What is the overall setting of this image?” is answered “Two,” an action question is also answered “Two,” and some stated k-values disagree with the number of listed capabilities. Other examples include capabilities that are plainly unnecessary for answering the question. These errors undermine reliance on Gemini self-verification.

Reproducibility and efficiency accounting remain incomplete: training hyperparameters, hardware, seeds, complete prompt interfaces, and code/data artifacts are absent or only promised. “Sample” ambiguously mixes image-level records with multiple question-answer turns, and the claimed 90% reduction is not accompanied by end-to-end training-time or compute comparisons that include synthetic-data generation. Licensing, privacy, and bias considerations for releasing regenerated LLaVA images and annotations are also not discussed.

The evaluation is broader than is typical for a data-curation paper: eight principal benchmarks, numerous equal-size selection baselines, the full 665K-sample baseline, scaling experiments, capability ablations, and knowledge-intensive evaluations.

The complexity-matched synthetic control, k-range ablation, instruction-data mixture study, token analysis, generation-cost disclosure, and experiment with an open-source generator are useful attempts to investigate the source and practicality of the gains.
The headline result is promising: the 65K-sample mixture attains 100.18% of the paper's aggregate relative score for full-data training, substantially exceeding the random 65K subset.
weaknesses: The central k-value is not validated as a reliable measure. The proposed capabilities overlap substantially, and Gemini-2.0-Flash generates the questions, verifies them, and later annotates their complexity. There is no human annotation study, inter-annotator agreement, independent-model validation, or estimate of precision/recall for capability labels. Consequently, self-consistency of one proprietary model is treated as ground truth.

The manuscript's own examples expose serious data-quality problems. In Figure 12, “What is the overall setting of this image?” and an action-recognition question are both answered “Two”; a purported k=5 example lists six capabilities. Several Figure 13 labels count capabilities already supplied by the wording—for example, “What vehicle is the person riding?” need not recognize the riding action to answer “motorcycle.” These examples directly undermine both answer correctness and the claimed exact capability verification.

The headline comparison is statistically fragile. Only single runs are reported, without error bars or significance tests. COMPACT's aggregate advantage over full-data training is merely 0.18 relative points; it wins four of eight benchmarks but loses the other four, including roughly 9.3% on CV-Bench and 6.7% on MME. Given training and evaluator variance, the evidence supports approximate parity at best, not an overall improvement.

The causal claim that higher k drives performance remains insufficiently isolated. COMPACT simultaneously changes complexity, capability balance, teacher-generated wording, filtering, answer length, and response style. The COMPACT-llava control is valuable but is run only at the smaller 16K synthetic budget, changes both k and capability distributions, and has no uncertainty estimates. The k-range ablation covers only three benchmarks and likewise uses single runs.

The study demonstrates limited generality: one LLaVA-v1.5-7B student, one LoRA training configuration, and one source dataset. It does not test another student architecture or scale, nor a standard compositional-generalization benchmark or held-out capability combinations. Broad benchmark averages therefore do not directly establish improved compositional reasoning.

Reproducibility is inadequate for a top-tier result. “Official settings” substitutes for exact optimization and hardware details; decoding, benchmark prompts, judge models, baseline implementations, random seeds, and the precise Gemini endpoint/version are missing. Data release is only promised. The quality-analysis sample size is also unspecified, despite reporting rejection percentages.

The 32K budget is described as the minimum needed to match full performance, but no validation-only selection protocol is given, suggesting possible tuning on reported test benchmarks. There is also no image/question contamination audit. Training cost is not compute-matched, and the proprietary Gemini generation cost is excluded from the principal efficiency claim.

The novelty is moderate: the method is capability-conditioned synthetic instruction generation coupled with a count-based complexity heuristic, close to prior compositional augmentation and atomic-skill decomposition. Stronger validation of the heuristic and substantially broader evidence would be needed to elevate this into a compelling top-tier contribution.
